answer.summary: Ipsen says breadth helps PMs diversify their skills and maximize future opportunities, especially if they want to lead product; it means working across different product areas rather than specializing in just one. She also recommends varied experience across types and stages of companies. [S1, S2]

sections.heading: Why breadth matters
sections.content: Ipsen says PMs who hope to become product leaders—potentially a head-of-product role—should touch different components and aspects of product. That broadens their skill set and helps maximize opportunities later in their careers. [S1, S2]

sections.heading: What varied experience can look like
sections.content: The interviewer’s examples, which Ipsen confirms, include working on platform, user-facing, and internal-tools teams. She also recommends diversifying experience across entrepreneurial work, such as starting something, and more established companies where PMs can learn best practices. [S2]

sections.heading: Caveat and additional benefit
sections.content: Breadth is not the only valid path: Ipsen says people who want to specialize in areas such as growth or ads can do so, and those skills are needed too. Lenny adds that variety can make someone a better PM by exposing them to how different products are built and teams operate; Ipsen agrees. [S2]
